top_reviews.title: A Modern Golden Age Mystery
top_reviews.text:
I love period mysteries, Nero Wolfe, Perry Mason, Sam Spade, and so on. These were truly from a "golden age," and they have a supremely different flavor than most current mysteries. Detectives in the golden age had less technology to use and abuse, and by and large they were driven by a personal hatred for bruised morality; they were fighters for the cause of right in a world that often spun off into wrong. The books tended to be circumspect about the portrayal of wrong, with less in-your-face violence and language. In short, I am happy to read most period mysteries, but most modern mysteries are not worth my time.

This mystery is new, but it is written as they were in the golden age, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. This was the first book I read from this author, but my next step is to get the rest of her mysteries. I am grateful to have a new source for great mystery writing. I am also pleased to find an author who is meticulous in her copyediting. I have a journalism background, and mistakes in copyediting grate on me. I didn't find one mistake through this whole book. It seems to have been a labor of love in more than one way.

top_reviews.title: I didn't beta read this one . . .
top_reviews.text:
Frankly, I didn't believe Renee could turn what had been an interesting character from a prior book into the protagonist of his own series, and I didn't want to be disappointed.

Reed Fergurson and his various friends are so well written that they feel like friends. Dewey Webb, a noir character from post WW2, didn't seem to be the sort of hero who would appeal to modern readers.

I was wrong!

The world of Mr. Webb - lacking the Internet, relying on pay phones, demanding brain power instead of computers - is straight out of a black and white Bogie film. Dames in trouble, shady characters, the carefully researched clothing and scenes, Ms. Pawlish has the era down flat.

I see other reviewers have given the plots away, so all I can add is an apology for doubting.

top_reviews.title: Dewey Webb, a master of mystery
top_reviews.text: When I started reading the novels written by Renee Pawlish I chose the "This Doesn't Happen in the Movies" a Reed Ferguson mystery.  Immediately I was hooked so I bought every other one in the series I could find and joined the author's newsletter.  When I received notice of Web of Deceit I was primed to enjoy it before I read it, but the book is so much more than I expected.  I absolutely love the film noir aspect of her writing and I see parallels between Sam Spade, Mike Hammer and others but the best part of Ms. Pawlish's character is the fact that he is a man who cares.  Sure he's scarred by his experiences in WWII and he has some rough edges.  He's not afraid to use his fists when necessary or display his gun to intimidate but he is such a likable person.  The story revolves around a husband who really loves his wife and hires Dewey to find out why her personality has changed.  Why is she so jumpy and secretive now?  What is she hiding?  Some of the plot line was predictable but even that didn't take anything away from the story because the twists and turns this story takes kept me anxious to read more.  One of the other things I particularly like about this story is that Dewey Webb is a family man.  He loves his wife and son and they love him.  He doesn't spend time worrying that she might leave him and take his son.  He does however show her in all their interactions that he loves her and wants to provide a good life for her and their son.  Dewey is first introduced in a Reed Ferguson novella called "Back Story".  I read "Back Story" after I read "Web of Deceit".  I'm glad I did it that way but I'll reserve my reasons why.  Suffice it to say that information in "Back Story" made my enjoyment and appreciation of "Web of Deceit" bitter sweet, however, I am looking forward to the next adventure with Dewey--the sooner the better!!
